records: Alexandria... Quite a lively port, with all these ships. Hm? What's that?
Preserve the busy harbor observation and interruption; use the bound Alexandria label.
No... Not this one, either. My beloved Elysion! Where are you!?
Cesare searches for his named ship; Elysion renders the source proper name, not a new vessel.
Is he looking for something?
Charles asks about the conspicuous search.
Seems so. You there, looking for something?
Hodram answers Charles, then directly approaches Cesare.
A ship, sir. My Elysion!
Retain Cesare's earnest formality and ownership claim.
Keep Hodram's questioning beat before the explanation.
The Elysion and I once sailed the seven seas.
Preserve the personal bond with the ship and broad travel claim.
But pirates attacked us. I survived, but they took the Elysion...
Retain survival and capture of the ship; do not claim it was destroyed.
And you've been looking for her ever since?
Charles checks the reason for the search.
Yes. I've searched port after port, but... Nothing yet.
Keep the unsuccessful search without inventing elapsed years or a specific route.
You said you sailed the seven seas. Have you been all over the world?
Hodram follows up on experience rather than assuming an exact itinerary.
Yes. Asia, the New World... I've visited many countries.
Retain the two explicit regions and general travel experience.
What was your position aboard ship?
Hodram asks about the former role.
Captain, of course, sir!
Captain is explicit; preserve Cesare's enthusiastic formality without adding a military rank.
Knowledge of distant lands, and experience as a captain...
Hodram weighs the two qualifications before recruiting.
Then how about this? Join my ship and help me with my work.
Preserve the proposal to serve aboard Hodram's ship, not immediate command of another fleet.
As we travel the world, we should be able to find your ship, too.
Keep the hopeful expectation, not a guarantee of a specific discovery.
Ha ha! Admiral {MACRO:FI}, I thought you might say that!
Charles recognizes Hodram's recruiting habit; preserve the exact name macro.
R-really!? I'd be most grateful, sir!
Cesare accepts eagerly while retaining his distinctive formality.
Come along. I'll show you aboard. I'm {MACRO:FI} {MACRO:FA}. I'll be counting on you.
Preserve both macros, the introduction and expectation of help.
Cesare Tony, sir!
Use the exact established full-name binding rather than an improvised surname.
I'm glad it worked out, Cesare. Charles Rochefort. A pleasure to meet you.
Keep Charles's warm congratulations and separate self-introduction.
Oh, Admiral. Might I offer you some advice on choosing ships?
This begins an optional tutorial; do not fold refusal and accepted advice into one sequence.
Of course! My apologies. You have your own principles! A splendid thing, sir!
The refusal branch respects the player's own approach with Cesare's exaggerated politeness.
I'll begin preparations to sail, then. Until later!
The refusal branch closes with departure preparations, not the tutorial.
Well, then...
Keep the separate accepted-tutorial opening.
While you're simply signing contracts with more towns and extending your trade routes, there's no need to buy ships. With a one percent contract, you can only buy one to five units of trade goods.
Preserve one percent and the one-to-five limit; literal percentages use words, not unsafe percent bytes.
Once your market share grows and you can buy more goods, it's time to buy another ship.
Connect ship purchases to increased available trade volume.
The first things to consider are size and price.
Retain the two explicit selection criteria.
Choose a ship that suits your market share and your funds. Otherwise, you'll need more sailors without being able to buy enough goods to fill her.
Preserve the mismatch between extra crew cost and unused capacity.
Price will give you an idea of size. Below 5,000 means a small ship; 10,000 to 20,000, a medium ship; and over 50,000, a large ship.
Keep the exact thresholds and unstated price gaps; do not turn them into continuous ranges.
Small ships are very cheap. Even when funds are tight, they make it easy to increase your fleet's cargo capacity.
Retain the affordability and additional carrying capacity.
After trading for a while, when you have more money to spare, switch to medium ships.
Keep the staged purchasing recommendation without a new required profit threshold.
Medium ships come with two or three masts. Three-masted ships are faster, of course, but they need more sail handlers.
Preserve both mast counts and the speed-versus-crew tradeoff; use the bound Sail Handler term.
Refitting can give you the maximum of five cargo holds. If you don't plan to fight for a while, you won't need marine quarters or batteries.
Retain the five-hold maximum and conditional removal of combat rooms; Quarters/Battery are the current UI labels.
To open routes to distant towns across the ocean, add more supply holds. They'll let you sail much farther.
Supplies extend sailing range; do not substitute cargo storage or guarantee arrival anywhere.
If you're going to pick a fight with another faction, though, you'll need large ships.
Keep the recommendation tied to conflict with another power.
At least equip your flagship with marine quarters and armed batteries. Winning sea battles will be difficult otherwise.
Retain the minimum flagship recommendation, both combat facilities and qualified difficulty.
Beyond that, it depends on your funds. Two medium ships cost less than one large ship and can carry more goods.
Preserve the specific two-to-one price and cargo comparison.
You'll eventually switch to large ships, but if you plan to form regional fleets, you may want to keep your old medium ships instead of selling them.
Retain future regional-fleet use as a reason to keep the older ships.
That concludes my advice. I'll begin preparations to sail. Until later!
Close only the accepted tutorial branch with its own preparation line.
Where in the world can my Elysion have gone?
Cesare remains worried about the same missing ship.
It's troubling that pirates took her. They generally strip a ship of her gold and cargo, then abandon her.
Gerhard describes a general practice, not proof that this particular ship was destroyed.
Oh... No...
Retain Cesare's dismay at the possibility.
Gerhard, about the ship... We've had word of a recent sighting near Lisbon.
Keep the report's location and recency; no eyewitness certainty is added.
What!?
Gerhard reacts to the new lead.
What did you say!? The Elysion's near here!?
Cesare checks the hopeful report eagerly.
Right, let's search the harbor.
Retain the initial search proposal.
Right, let's search the harbor again.
The repeated-search variant is a separate occurrence and must retain again.
Yes, sir.
Cesare agrees in his established formal voice.
No luck. She's not here, either...
Keep the unsuccessful search at this particular spot.
Don't look so downhearted. We'll find her someday...
Gerhard reassures Cesare without a new concrete lead.
That's right. I'll help you look, too.
Charles's optional encouragement offers help with the search.
She should be somewhere nearby. The rest is down to your luck. Don't lose hope.
Keep the nearby inference, luck motif and encouragement.
Yes...
Cesare's subdued answer precedes the discovery.
No sign of her, Cesare. Any luck your way?
Gerhard asks about Cesare's part of the search.
Retain the exact intentional inarticulate-shock symbols; this is comedy, not an encoding defect.
What is it, Cesare?
Gerhard responds to the wordless outburst.
E-E-E-Elysion! It's the Elysion!
Preserve the stammer and ecstatic ship recognition.
What's happened? Have you found her?
Gerhard checks the reason for the outburst.
Looks like it. He gave a strange cry and ran aboard that ship...
Charles reports Cesare's conspicuous action, not confirmed ownership yet.
Claudio: W-who is this guy!? A thief!?
Keep Claudio's explicit embedded heading and startled suspicion.
Claudio (explicit FE heading)
Rafael: A thief!?
Preserve the approved Rafael name in the embedded heading.
Rafael (explicit FE heading)
Cesare: Elysion!
Cesare is calling the ship's name, not introducing himself despite the heading.
Cesare (explicit FE heading)
This seems to have caused quite a commotion...
Charles reacts to the misunderstanding aboard the other ship.
This is bad. We must stop him! Cesare!
Gerhard intervenes to prevent escalation.
Cesare! Calm down! Calm down!
Retain the repeated urgent calming call.
Ah... I'm sorry. The moment I saw the Elysion, my mind went blank...
Cesare apologizes for losing control, without inventing amnesia or illness.
What the hell is going on?
Keep Claudio's rough demand for an explanation.
I'm Rafael Castor, of the Castor Company. And you are?
Bind real actor0 to Rafael, preserving his company introduction without inventing a family relationship.
My apologies. Gerhard Adernkatz, of {MACRO:FO}.
Preserve the full bound name and exact faction macro.
Oh! You're with {MACRO:FO}...
Rafael recognizes the faction; preserve its runtime substitution.
And this is Cesare Tony.
Gerhard introduces the distraught ship owner by the established name.
I'm sorry. I got carried away...
Keep Cesare's second apology to the other crew.
Why did you come aboard our ship?
Arcadius, not Fernando, asks the source question.
This is the Elysion. She used to be my ship...
Cesare claims former ownership rather than accusing the present crew of theft.
What are you talking about? This is our ship!
Claudio defends the present crew's possession.
Wait, Clau. He might be telling the truth.
Preserve Rafael's familiar source nickname for Claudio without a new relationship claim.
We found her abandoned, washed up on the shore, remember?
Rafael supplies the source-supported discovery circumstances; no purchase or theft is invented.
But... Can you offer any proof?
Arcadius asks for evidence rather than dismissing the claim.
Proof... Cesare? Can you think of anything?
Gerhard turns the evidence question to the former owner.
Proof...? Oh, yes!
Cesare recalls a distinguishing mark.
There should be something I carved into her side. The words 'Good Luck'!
Good Luck is a carved inscription proving identity, not the ship's name; ordinary ASCII is intentional here.
Hmm... Claudio, would you check the side of the ship?
Arcadius delegates the physical evidence check.
Me? Why me? What a pain...
Claudio grumbles at the errand in his blunt voice.
We need to establish the truth! A man loses respect when he grumbles over every little thing.
Retain Arcadius's insistence and masculine-pride rebuke without adding a rank.
Tch... Fine. Always making me do everything...
Claudio agrees while continuing to complain.
I checked. Unbelievable... It's really carved there.
Preserve the actual verification of the inscription, not an unsupported ownership guess.
It is!?
Cesare checks the positive result eagerly.
You found her!
Charles's optional response celebrates the successful identification.
I'm glad, Cesare.
Gerhard warmly acknowledges the discovery.
Y-yes...
Cesare's emotion keeps the answer hesitant.
Then this ship...
Arcadius leaves the ownership implication unfinished.
Damn... We can't do without this ship now.
Claudio states the present crew's practical dependence, not a right to confiscate it.
Hmm... I can see that. What will you do, Cesare?
Gerhard recognizes their predicament and leaves the decision to Cesare.
...Let's go. Just seeing the Elysion again is enough for me...
Critical progression: Cesare first chooses to leave the ship with its current crew.
Please... Take good care of her.
His parting request concerns care for the Elysion, not payment.
Cesare...
Keep Charles's subdued optional response to the sacrifice.
Are you sure?
Gerhard checks whether Cesare accepts leaving the ship.
Yes...
Cesare confirms before Rafael changes the outcome.
...Please, wait. She's your ship, isn't she?
Rafael stops Cesare's departure on his own initiative.
Well, yes... She used to be...
Cesare qualifies former ownership rather than demanding return.
Then please, take the Elysion.
Critical agency: Rafael voluntarily returns the ship after Cesare offered to leave it.
Hey! What are you saying? It's our ship! What are we supposed to do!?
Claudio raises the practical consequence of giving up their vessel.
We'll... figure something out. I understand how Cesare feels. Come on, let's give her back.
Preserve Rafael's empathy and uncertain practical solution; invent no replacement ship or compensation.
...Ahh. You softhearted fool... All right.
Claudio relents with affectionate exasperation, not a new refusal.
...R-really? You're sure?
Cesare can scarcely believe the generous offer.
Yes. We'll leave her tied up here at the dock for you.
Rafael specifies the handover location without inventing a sale or transfer fee.
Thank you! I can sail with the Elysion again!
Keep gratitude and renewed companionship with his ship.
I'm so glad!
Charles shares Cesare's happiness in the optional response.
My thanks as well. Such generosity in one so young...
Gerhard explicitly admires Rafael's generosity and youth; no precise age is supplied.
Oh, no, I...
Rafael responds modestly and leaves the thought unfinished.
No need for modesty. You're cut from the same cloth as my admiral. I can tell.
Localize the shared-spirit metaphor rather than literal smell; do not turn admiration into kinship.
Rafael, it has been an honor to meet you. Farewell.
Gerhard closes respectfully using the approved Rafael spelling.
Thank you so very much!
Cesare's final emphatic gratitude closes the complete exchange.
